title: The Punjab years
hookLine: violence by militants and by police killed people across Punjab; a human-rights worker, Jaswant Singh Khalra, documented disappearances and was killed

cards: A ledger in a city office: dates, firewood, and a line that says unidentified. Then another line, and another. The cremation ground keeps records of the wood it buys to burn the dead.
A man from Amritsar named Jaswant Singh Khalra asked to see those records. He began adding up the lines marked unidentified, and he began asking a simple, dangerous question: who were they?
These were the years when Punjab burned from more than one side.

teach.b: First, the violence from one side.

After the June and the November, armed militants fighting for a separate Sikh state called Khalistan killed police and officials, and they also killed ordinary people: Hindus, and Sikhs who disagreed with them.
Buses were stopped. Markets were bombed. Second, the violence from the other.
Police fighting the militants were given wide powers, and young Sikh men were picked up, tortured, killed in staged encounters, or simply disappeared.
Families went to police stations and were told their sons had never been there. Both are part of the record, and Punjab's families carry both. Third, the counting.

Jaswant Singh Khalra worked for the human rights wing of the Akali Dal. He went through cremation ground records in Amritsar district and found bodies cremated as unidentified, lines he believed were the disappeared.
He published what he found and spoke about it, in India and abroad. Then he himself was taken from outside his home and killed. Police officers were later convicted for his abduction and murder.

teach.h: ANG 723: TRUTH AT THE TIME FOR TRUTH.
teach.b: In the hymns Guru Nanak sang about the violence of Babur's armies, at Ang 723, he says that he speaks the word of truth, and will tell the truth at the time for truth.
Khalra did not pick up a weapon. He picked up a ledger. He is remembered for that.

how: Sikhs remember Jaswant Singh Khalra as a defender of human rights; families of the disappeared and human rights groups continue to seek records and justice for those killed in these years.

games.why: Khalra published what he found and spoke about it, at home and abroad. it cost him his life.

practice: Bring to mind one person who told a hard truth when it cost them: a whistleblower, a journalist, a friend who said what no one else would, maybe someone in your own family.

Breathe in and see their face, breathe out and thank them silently, then simply hold one small truth you've kept quiet, with no need to act on it now. If you pray, let Waheguru go with the breath out.

wordCard.voice: Khalra. The Amritsar man who read cremation ledgers, counted the disappeared of the Punjab years, and was killed for it. Today's word.
